title: Case Forms of aki: akit, akinek, akik

sections.content: 'aki' behaves like any other Hungarian noun-like word: it takes case endings depending on the job it does inside its OWN clause — not the job its antecedent does in the main sentence. So far you've only seen 'aki' as a subject ('aki uralkodott' — who ruled). Now meet its other everyday forms: 'akit' (whom, as a direct object) and 'akinek' (to whom, or whose, marking a dative or possessor role), plus the plural 'akik' and 'akiket'.

sections.title: aki's case forms
rows: to whom / whose (dative or possessor, singular)

items.spanish: IV. Béla, akit a tatárjárás sújtott a legjobban, az ország újjáépítésébe kezdett.
items.english: Béla IV, whom the Mongol invasion hit hardest, began rebuilding the country.

items.spanish: Az ispán, akinek a megye igazgatása volt a feladata, a király nevében ítélkezett.
items.english: The ispán, whose task was administering the county, judged in the king's name.

items.spanish: Azok a nemesek, akik a várak építését szorgalmazták, jól látták a jövő veszélyeit.
items.english: Those nobles who urged the building of castles saw the dangers ahead clearly.

sections.content: Work out the case of 'aki' from inside its own clause, ignoring the main sentence. In 'az ispán, akinek a megye igazgatása volt a feladata', 'az ispán' is the subject of the whole sentence, but inside the relative clause 'akinek' is a possessor ('akinek a feladata' = 'whose task'), so it takes the -nek ending — the two clauses are grammatically independent of each other.
